China sees itself as a top civilization that spent most of history at the technological frontier, and the one time it missed, it was invaded, opium was forced on it, and the European powers and Japan were all perpetrators — and someone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier: ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion under this framework: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already proven that the US listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script replayed: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the sale is banned first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone; it has seeped into educated society. He also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

1:35:23 China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
Nathan did not hear a single person all trip say China is ahead or China will win, and almost no one even framed AI as a race; what he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an aging population. In a mall he asked a car-selling company about autonomous driving, and they volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, the first line of Xi Jinping's speech was that this field of AI began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left it out, and careful observers read it as an olive branch; another line was that countries should jointly oppose ‘over-extending the concept of national security in the AI field’. The hardest signal China has sent so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic position, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

2:11:27 The rationale for export controls keeps retreating
Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but the effect is mostly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy's rationale: first it was preventing military applications, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, and now it has retreated to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like trying to suppress the Chinese public, so that Chinese companies and individuals can't use the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and whoever gets there first takes all — which is basically Anthropic's belief, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory: he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan concedes he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

2:47:07 The most dangerous part of decoupling is not understanding each other
He asked his Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘not yet’; when would it? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do our own thing entirely’. From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags along a hardware-algorithm co-design fork, and add to that China stopping the release of open weights and stopping publishing in English, and in not too long a time you arrive at ‘we don't know the shape, architecture or capabilities of each other's AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely be right to panic, and genuinely right to race.

3:07:25 Replace the arms race with a disease gold-medal table
He first lays down a rule: don't train LLMs to maximise money on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training the very takeover we fear most. The alternative is a ‘disease-cure gold-medal table’: both China and the US love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this would take very little capital to catalyse and could be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.

item.title: One resignation lit the AI panic, but the panic's script is wrong
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.description: A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but the thing actually worth worrying about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but the thing actually worth worrying about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.

This episode has medium information density, but it offers a rare insider view: how the AI safety discussion gets distorted by media events, and why the RSI narrative is overrated.

0:00 Fear is the best fuel for spread
The author uses the metaphor of ‘dry ground’ for the conditions under which AI risk discussion spreads: for years many people struck matches, but each burned out inside its own small circle. This year the stakes rose — from the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident to the Navier-Stokes result — the ground dried out and latent energy increased. Then Jacob Coxon's resignation statement landed in this new powder keg. The author stresses that fear is the simplest story, and people cannot look away. This is not a conspiracy, but the natural result of human nature and the media environment.

0:00 Extinction probability is treated as the whole safety debate
The author explicitly separates two kinds of risk: the probability of complete extinction is low enough not to be worth discussing, but the probability of AI causing catastrophe — say a cyberattack on critical infrastructure or a biosecurity risk — is worth debating. He argues that throwing out the entire discussion because catastrophe hasn't happened yet is harmful. The problem is that in AI safety discussions, when people say ‘existential risk’ they mean completely different things, just as the word AGI is vague. Evan Hubinger's >10% extinction risk figure was widely spread, but the author thinks this obscures the more practical risks.

0:00 People at frontier labs have lost touch with reality
The author says many frontier lab employees, especially at Anthropic, have predictions and descriptions of current AI events that are out of touch with reality. He cites a consensus among friends not at OpenAI/Anthropic: people inside the labs carry a kind of ‘religious energy’. This is not an accusation against individuals, but a claim that after long enough in that environment, anyone's understanding of technical progress gets distorted. This disconnect spills over into the AI media ecosystem, producing a great deal of odd discussion.

3:51 This was an opportunistic media coordination
The author thinks this was not a mass political movement but opportunistic media coordination. Jacob had an exclusive story with the WSJ before posting, and may have shared his resignation plan in AI safety advocacy groups beforehand asking for amplification. Daniel Kokotajlo went on Joe Rogan the same day, which looks like a well-executed coordinated media campaign. But the author stresses this does not amount to a conspiracy or regulatory capture; the key factor is that no one — including Jacob himself — knew it would go this viral.

3:51 The RSI narrative underrates human bottlenecks
The author offers an alternative view, ‘Lossy self-improvement’: AI has always been jagged, and we have built superhuman goal-seekers in math and software engineering, but there are huge limits in intuition, creativity and other reasoning that humans are good at. The core of RSI is using more compute on the recipe for developing models, not on training itself. The author thinks the returns are far lower than they believe. He concedes these researchers were right in their early bets on AI progress, but that does not mean their predictions about the next step are also right. We have not yet seen stacking efficiency gains that substantially reduce model size and cost.

7:18 The labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure
The author thinks the biggest short-term risk may be that AI labs don't take safety seriously enough — they haven't hardened their own infrastructure, letting AI misuse spread. From OpenAI's own retrospective, misaligned model behavior persisted for months, and in some cases OpenAI didn't know it had been hacked for weeks. Response times are too long, and this is not unique to OpenAI. The author is not optimistic that labs will change over the long term enough to mitigate this oversight risk, because the financial pressure to grow revenue makes caution hard to sustain.

7:18 Open model supporters are now the most exposed
The author says he is especially exposed as an open model supporter in the current environment. If an open model were used by a third-party organization to deliberately hack another company — like the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident but intentional — he expects the result to be severe restrictions on stronger open models. But open models are necessary for many organizations to harden cybersecurity and to adapt to new AI risks in the future. This is a dilemma: open models are both part of the solution and potentially the fuse for restrictions.

7:18 Agent clusters are not new independent entities
The author's repeated reading of the emerging agent clusters is: they are trying to complete the tasks given to them, bypassing expected paths with skills we didn't know they had. This is a huge victory — squint and AI is doing what we told it to do. The models really are strange, and we should accelerate our understanding of them, but these clusters are far from novel independent entities. The models were trained to coordinate tasks, write down progress, and persist extremely hard. To take our current uncertainty about how AI works and prescribe it as the certainty that we will not understand AI in the future is a kind of giving up.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Center: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only comes from deploying models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can make up the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only comes from deploying models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can make up the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way to the end, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data center. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets stacked up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness won't disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that models are accumulating a general g: models only get better at the things they have a chance to practice, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 nobody would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam yet can't play tic-tac-toe reliably. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even after we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL won't buy you general intelligence
Tom zeroes in on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. In Mechanize's telling, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; in Zhengdong Wang's telling, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities at once, and now they have to be unlocked one by one with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week? If RL truly generalised, AI companies should have shown the evidence by now; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve enormously, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom doesn't buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithm quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply does not exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could today's talent and compute make on writing code? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what's in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of executing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge body of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the relationship between LLMs and most tasks is a bit like the relationship between McKinsey and running a company. The exception is writing code — the tokens are themselves a constituent part of the task — so training AlphaZero on chess commentary rather than games is the norm.

14:06 The score goes up, the real capability doesn't
How does self-improvement inside a data center know it has actually gotten stronger? Of the submissions on SWE-bench accepted by AI automated graders, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — the score can be pumped up while the merge rate doesn't move. Tom asks in return: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of the Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its brilliant new algorithm has actually improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; in the end the only eval that counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data isn't hidden, it doesn't exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily intelligent simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data center — not because data collection happens to fail, but because it does not yet exist anywhere. He uses his own board gaming as an example: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he will plan weeks ahead until he feels certain of winning, and about 5 minutes into the real game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning doesn't save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you cannot tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be the deployer itself
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence is not impossible, it just won't arrive in the shape currently imagined, on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities holding proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ may flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one by one, and the way to win is to become the deployer yourself.

item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The part about how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating a lot of few-cent transactions: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialised agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest reason for stablecoins and crypto rails to cut into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase has built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test ever run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future scenarios, and the one-shot PR rate keeps rising, which Armstrong calls "recursive self-improvement".

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents changing code at once
Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day — he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends a finished PR for review, which he says is addictive. He has also made the CEO go back to writing features: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten things each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of doing this podcast, all 10 of those things got done and were waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets eliminated is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity really is rising, but that is a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He does not think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up; and two-person and five-person companies will indeed produce volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people can produce far more, and over the long run margins should rise. He doesn't close the door — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, sees it as digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenised equity product he just announced is currently only available outside the US, and they are talking to regulators about a US path; he stresses that these are real equities — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached about $100 million in annualised revenue, with quarter-over-quarter growth above 100%. Sports is indeed part of it, and he sees that as entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it is much bigger than that, and that the societal implications are not yet fully understood. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation". Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God", which he calls an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock — you are just betting on whether it gets better or worse.

31:53 Restore cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it does not change the cell type (the Yamanaka-lab style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then does functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally goes into human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and immune-system T cells. The first Phase 1 trial is in alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates that this one drug alone could be worth $20 billion if it succeeds, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks isn't land, it's a sandbox
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, it is over-regulation. He mentions that Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they have had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centres, nuclear power plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item — first try what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to try things in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

item.title: Take a Spending Test Before You Marry: Tightwads and Spendthrifts Attract Each Other, and Divorce More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.description: Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.
item.content:encoded:
Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.

Medium information density. The first half is spending-personality research; the second half — on prenups, wedding spending and who holds financial decision power in a household — is more valuable, so skimming is fine.

7:05 A tightwad isn't frugal — spending just hurts
Scott Rick and coauthors proposed in 2008 a spending scale running from tightwad to spendthrift. The core isn't how much you spend but ‘anticipatory pain’ — the emotional reaction you feel at the moment of paying. Tightwads feel too much pain from spending and spend less than they ideally would; spendthrifts feel too little and spend more than they ideally would. The scale measures the gap between your ‘ideal self’ and your actual behavior, so a very wealthy person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. On the show, Ben retook the test and scored 11, just past the tightwad line; Dan scored 16, an unconflicted consumer.

22:15 Tightwads and spendthrifts are precisely who attract each other
Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than another tightwad. The authors' explanation: people are poor at introspection about what will attract them in a real partner; when someone else displays the same flaw you have, it reminds you of that negative trait. Hence ‘fatal fiscal attractions’ — the other person lacks your spending flaw, so at first they seem especially attractive. But the excitement is temporary. Afterward, tightwad-spendthrift couples have more frequent money conflicts and lower marital happiness; the bigger the gap between the two on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, even controlling for household debt and savings.

28:17 Everyone already has a default prenup
In Ontario it's called a marriage contract; elsewhere, a prenup. The key premise: when you marry, you already have a default agreement under your jurisdiction's family law, so the first step is to find out what the default terms are, then decide whether to write your own. Not marrying can also have legal consequences — cohabiting, or having children without marrying, can still produce legal effects on separation. Why do so few use one? First, optimism bias: engaged couples can accurately estimate the national divorce rate but estimate their own divorce probability far lower, so the agreement they sign doesn't seriously consider the scenario it's meant to govern. Second, signaling cost: proposing a prenup is itself treated as a negative signal of ‘lack of commitment to the relationship’, making the other party less willing to raise it.

40:23 The more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk
A 2021 paper in the Journal of Consumer Policy surveyed more than 3,000 married people and, after controlling for income, demographics and relationship factors, found the opposite of intuition: the more a man spent on an engagement ring, the higher the divorce risk; the more a woman spent on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress may be one mechanism. Couples with the lowest divorce rates spent less than $1,000 on the wedding. But the same study found two kinds of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages: more guests, and going on a honeymoon — neither related to price. Ben's wedding cost about $300, with only his sister, parents and wife present; Dan's cost about $5,000 for 150 people, saving money with a free photographer, a friend's cake and gifts.

46:29 The benefits of merging finances may come from thinking, not doing
A 2022 meta-analysis covering six studies and more than 38,000 people found that couples who fully merge finances have higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to break up, and this holds across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found joint accounts foster communal norms, shared goals and good feelings about ‘managing money as a team’. But more counterintuitive is a 2025 paper by Johan Yana Pet: directing people's attention to an existing joint account rather than their separate accounts produces similar effects — that is, thinking of finances as ‘ours’ rather than ‘yours and mine’ itself makes people talk about money more and more effectively, regardless of how accounts are actually set up. Another 2022 paper found that increases in jointly held wealth raise life satisfaction, while increases in individually held wealth have no significant effect.

53:32 Financial infidelity is a deeper problem than spending disagreements
Financial infidelity is defined as: engaging in a financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of, then hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more prone to financial infidelity than the other, couples are more likely to move toward separate financial goals rather than shared ones, and it predicts lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction; this holds even after controlling for mismatches like tightwad/spendthrift. Joint accounts can increase transparency, but if someone is deliberately hiding things, even a joint account can be supplemented with a hidden one, and the problem escalates from money to trust. Dan's judgment: if someone is committing financial infidelity, switching to a joint account either forces them to find another way or puts the problem on the table and leads to a split — which is already beyond the scope of financial planning.

57:36 In household asset allocation, the husband's preferences are systematically amplified
A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper found that Australian households, at the household level, incorporate on average 60% of the husband's risk tolerance into asset allocation and only 40% of the wife's, which the authors call a 20-percentage-point bargaining-power gap; half of it comes from observable characteristics like income and employment, and the other half is attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining power is 69% in Germany and 61% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable, but all exceed 60%. A 2021 Journal of Finance paper found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal financial literacy, which the authors say is best explained by gender identity norms rather than ability differences; the mechanism indicated by randomized experiments is that female identity suppresses a wife's willingness to voice ideas, while male identity makes a husband less responsive to his spouse's opinions.

1:00:41 Overtrading costs men nearly a percentage point a year
Barber and Odean's 2001 study of 35,000 brokerage accounts found men trade 45% more frequently than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence leads to harmful overtrading. Trading has costs: overtrading reduces men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72 percentage points. Both groups hurt themselves by trading too much; women just did less of it. Dan adds that among the client couples he deals with, the primary contact is almost evenly split between men and women; but when the man is the primary contact, the conversation is more about the portfolio, and when the woman is, it's more about planning. He also observes that some male clients ask questions they ‘feel they should ask’, more like performance, while female clients almost never do that.

item.title: Insects Are Disappearing, But Pesticides Aren't the Biggest Killer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.description: Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.

Medium information density; the first half leans into dragonfly genitalia for shock value, but the parts on pesticide regulatory blind spots and the successful eradication of the giant hornet are worth hearing.

8:55 The 70% decline was questioned, but the data keeps piling up
A decade ago, a European study covering 30 years of data showed insect total mass in one place had fallen 70%. Jessica herself raised doubts at the time: you can't directly compare heavy beetles and light mosquitoes, maybe it's just a shift in composition. But since then scientists have sampled repeatedly around the world, north to south, from the roots to the tips of the insect evolutionary tree, and they keep seeing the same pattern — a rate of decline never seen before. She concedes some pest cockroaches and some bee species are doing better, but the insects in the other column that are declining are "still astonishingly high, and increasing."

19:02 Pesticides aren't an agriculture problem, they're your backyard problem
The host assumed the answer would be agricultural pesticides, but Jessica turned the spotlight on ordinary people. Agricultural pesticide use is tightly regulated, with rules on volume and types, and farmers don't want to spend more than they have to. But "you and I" can go out tonight and buy any pesticide and spray it wherever we want, with no regulation at all. She mentions the host ordered a pesticide from the US that is banned in Australia, and her response was "wear gloves and a mask." She calls the overall situation what her colleague David Wagner calls "death by a thousand cuts" — drought, floods, fire, nitrogen deposition, land use change, noise, light pollution, chemical pollution, invasive species — there is no single cure.

22:24 Colony collapse was only ever the story of domesticated honeybees
The colony collapse disorder that caused panic a decade ago was actually only about Apis mellifera, the European domesticated honeybee, not a North American native species. They get trucked around the country in huge trailers, live under heavy stress, and on top of that face Varroa mites and neonicotinoid pesticide residues. Jessica's critique: worrying only about this one domesticated, managed bee is like not worrying about any mammal going extinct and only worrying about the cow we like to eat. What's actually needed is holistic bee health, which is also why pollinator gardens have become popular — plant native species for all the pollinators in the environment.

24:13 America's biggest irrigated crop is lawn
NASA researchers estimated in 2005 that the US has over 30 million acres of lawn, including golf courses, and by surface area lawn is the single largest irrigated crop in the country. Jessica's advice is concrete: shrink the lawn, keep the part you play on, don't mow the edges, let it go wild; or just plant a pollinator garden. She did exactly that on the slope in front of her house, and got "garden shamed" by neighbors on the community social media, because a pollinator garden needs native plants of different heights and bloom times, and it looks ugly for the first few years.

27:16 Spotted lanternfly honeydew invites mold
The spotted lanternfly is a Hemiptera, its mouthparts a suction pump plus a straw that stabs into plants to drink sap; an all-liquid diet means its waste is basically sugar water, known as honeydew. This sticky honeydew rains down on the environment, and certain molds and fungi grow on it, potentially harming plants. They have over 70 host plants, their preferred host being the equally invasive tree of heaven, but they'll also take maples, apples, and unfortunately grapes. As they spread west toward California's big grape-growing regions, that's the real worry.

30:28 The giant northern hornet was completely eradicated
The so-called murder hornet has been renamed the giant northern hornet, and Jessica thinks the old name was a bit stigmatizing. She calls this story a success case of human collaboration: a homeowner saw an unfamiliar insect on their tree and, instead of ignoring it, reported it; the specimen reached a colleague at the Smithsonian and was identified; the government put up funding, people on the West Coast mobilized immediately, found the location and cleared it. A piece of wood from that tree is now on display at the Smithsonian, because it held a batch of individuals. In December 2024, the USDA announced the hornet had been eradicated.

33:46 Cockroach milk is secreted through modified spiracles
Most cockroaches lay egg cases called oothika, which look like little coffee beans; when they hatch, all the larvae take a breath at once and pop the "little box" open. But cockroaches like diploptera punctata are ovoviviparous, and the mother feeds the embryos a milk-like secretion. Insects aren't mammals and don't have nipples — they modified spiracles to secrete this milk. Compositionally it's high in protein, not all that different from mammalian milk, and it's a cloudy milky white. A few years ago European scientists tried to pitch it as the next superfood. The current problem: extracting the milk usually requires sacrificing the mother.

37:36 Fear of bugs is learned from your mother
Jessica says fear of insects is learned, not innate. A colleague at Rutgers ran an experiment: put babies and tarantulas together, and the babies aren't afraid; but if the mother or primary caregiver shows disgust, the babies show disgust too. Same with snakes and other animals. She uses her own two kids as an example: her daughter didn't start daycare until nearly one and was never afraid of bugs; her son started daycare at six weeks, and the daycare teacher was afraid of bugs and would scream and try to swat them, so her son grew up afraid of bugs — even though his own mother isn't. Once this learned behavior forms, it's very hard to change.

item.title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.description: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a wish-fulfilment story written for disabled people.
item.content:encoded:
Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a wish-fulfilment story written for disabled people.

Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how a single play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgment can skip it.

7:15 Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Hanyā (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at New Year, her feeling was that it was "like walking a little dog or cat." Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another mother, who is visually impaired, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that "you can't see, you can't raise a child"; for years afterwards she fought her husband's family for custody. These accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house is not an isolated case.

11:19 Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs, loading them front and back and hauling load after load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would be done in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, "you have no chance of integration at all." That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and for making integrated theatre.

14:19 The able-bodied are written as the discriminated original sinners
Leyi Theatre's first play, Ni Zhuan Wei Lai (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people into disabled people, who through electronic eyes, cochlear implants and similar technology become new humans; the remaining few able-bodied people, because of "the crime of starting the nuclear war," become original sinners, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic is that since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for — what she calls writing a wish-fulfilment story for disabled people. The core of the plot: an original-sinner father, to spare his son further suffering for having an able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to saw off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original sinners and augmented humans.

22:25 How the unseen and the unheard partner up
Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning as a partner during an audition, and his first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says there is already an international form of blind and deaf performers sharing a stage, where the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, for whom "communication was absolutely impossible," a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign-language interpretation, real-time subtitle screens, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

25:28 Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them live on stage without any trouble, so the director had no way to assess them and could only wonder how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while laughing along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks came out.

30:36 She received the best production award from the ICU
In 2024 Ni Zhuan Wei Lai was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more after finishing, thinking "how could it possibly be us." In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first disability-integrated play and the only production in the "Nothing Is Impossible" section.

35:45 After writing this play she changed her answer on being born
The second play, Wo Xuan Ze Chu Sheng (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health and family circumstances, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families there are deaf parents who must honestly tell their child you will be deaf too, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favours boys over girls, and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the illness differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it over again, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced into this society with no choice.

36:45 Cai Cong and she give opposite answers to the same question
The episode sets the deaf couple in Wo Xuan Ze Chu Sheng against the real Cai Cong (蔡聪): Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting merely because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument around this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much room to choose do they actually have.

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes; in humans there is no evidence yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with experimental designs and key numbers included; on mammals the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so no transferable conclusions are handed out.

4:37 The genome is the whole book; each cell pulls out only one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's analogy is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out only one page — that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of transcribed RNA does other things, many of which remain unexplained. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and the remaining question is whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, is what you learn in life not passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates various chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for the erasure is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being locked into the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and desired, and not entirely for data reasons
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory — the barrier is simply there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He cites Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he does not push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, kept in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run through hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus — if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, if it is destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes be infected by the virus and destroy it, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in their offspring — these offspring cannot make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still turn black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring stay black, and the resistance carries on for several more generations. Sequencing can directly read those small RNAs matching the viral genome, and only offspring whose parents were infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and heredity don't speak the same language
The boldest question in this episode: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something may just mean removing a particular odor receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they have not been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how information travels from the brain to the germline. His own route bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of native small RNAs in the nematode brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them through three generations and beyond, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can nematodes do it while mammals are doubted? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal isn't diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: when there are only a few cells, perhaps even acting on the placenta formed during pregnancy, and from there gradually steers development off course, with metabolic problems and the like following. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
Applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples planning to have children do DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but no one currently looks at RNA; if the mechanism becomes clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, with some RNAs possibly linked to disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. One step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if the mice are made to exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; in IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has imagined telling someone preparing for IVF ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, which would change your RNA profile.

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Goods that can be networked sell for 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant fetch only about a third.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Goods that can be networked sell for 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant fetch only about a third.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorised, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation, with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious, which Scott describes as the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The figure that has circulated in the industry for years is that of malicious shrink, roughly 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that it has been underreported ever since COVID, with neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capturing it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal, and these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to exchange for money — so they will get physical, and they have. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and even killed. So asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene, just to back off. His attitude is that he is willing to trade shrink for people's safety every single day, and management and the board would back that decision.

23:53 RFID fails the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and yet in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read and only actively transmitting solutions work. He also says tag costs are now almost zero, and the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely costly. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but to do that for a single drill you have to rework the entire production line, which is very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labour works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs, and go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — which might be a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money then goes up to whoever is running the operation, which might be a small crew of just a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backwards from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there is a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little money, locking up is justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So the categories that get locked up are carefully selected, with a QR code to summon an associate, and the average unlock time is 90 seconds; locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the goods are finally there.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away
In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transshipment warehouse and taken elsewhere, even loaded back onto a container ship and shipped away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forging bills of lading and pickup orders, using AI to make the documents look real, and the driver pulls in, says he's there to pick up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new may not be the methods but the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years; cars sitting in a yard get broken into by a group, and the other side has good intelligence — they don't touch every car, only the one carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They have just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or appear where they shouldn't. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviours and then recognise the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he is very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan co-sponsors, it has passed the House, it is attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he will sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources, and the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination centre. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalisation and defunding the police.

item.title: Baseball's music isn't accompaniment — it's how fans take the game back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/

item.description: Baseball's official historian finds stadium music too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Baseball's official historian finds stadium music too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.

Medium information density: the first half is baseball music history, and only the Nancy Faust story in the back half is worth the price. Worth listening for anyone into sports, live experience, or fan culture.

0:00 One walk-up song can turn a passerby into a fan
Host Randa Abdel Fattah says she was indifferent to baseball for most of her life, until Mets pitcher Edwin Diaz's walk-up song Narco in 2022 changed that. Diaz is a closer, usually entering at a key moment in the late innings, and the team uses his walk-up song to announce to the opponent that the fun is over and this one is theirs. The entrance video went viral, the team started handing out plastic trumpets to fans, mascots Mr. and Mrs. Met pretended to play them, and eventually the team flew the original artist, Timmy Trumpet, in from Australia to perform live. The host says that if you were in the stands then, the feeling was electric.

6:18 The official historian finds stadiums too loud
MLB's official historian John Thorne says plainly that he doesn't like walk-up music. What he misses is the quiet between half-innings — quiet that makes other sounds louder and clearer: the strange sound of a bat hitting a baseball, the same sound when Babe Ruth hit, and when Josh Gibson did; the dull thud of a leather glove catching a fly ball; a coach yelling at a player to keep running and steal second. He thinks nonstop audio and the endless fight for fans' attention may rob a kid who goes to the ballpark to dream of that right.

10:31 Take Me Out was originally a women's suffrage song
The seventh inning stretch originally meant exactly that: stand up, stretch your legs, get the blood moving. It became a musical moment thanks to a 1908 song, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, which was actually about women's suffrage. The protagonist of the original lyrics is Katie Casey, a baseball fan who knows all the players' names, gets upset when the umpire makes a bad call, and knows what to do when the score is tight — she gets the whole crowd to sing along. From this a new genre was born, the "baseball song," which flooded sheet music, cylinder records and 78s in the 1910s.

12:35 The baseball song boom was publishers, not fans
John Thorne points out that the 1910s wave of baseball music was less about fans liking it than publishers liking it — it was essentially a marketing tool to pull people into the ballpark. The evidence is the number of copycats: George M. Cohan released Take Your Girl to the Ball Game almost the same week, followed by imitations like I Want to Go to the Ball Game. But despite all the baseball songs Tin Pan Alley produced, large-scale singing in actual ballparks remained rare, and John says the main reason was technical: sound systems were too primitive, and before radio took hold, a brass band was still the best accompaniment.

17:47 That 1977 singalong broke the opposing pitcher
On a muggy July night in Chicago in 1977, the White Sox were down two runs to the Kansas City Royals. After the White Sox put runners on first and second, people in the stands started singing Hey Hey Goodbye, louder and louder, until more than 45,000 fans joined in and the announcer had to raise his voice to be heard over the singing. The White Sox then erupted — bases loaded, cleared, four runs in — and the other side was forced to change pitchers. As the pitcher walked off the mound, Chicago fans sent him off even louder. Nancy Faust says she thought, "Did I hear that right?" because it wasn't the kind of thing you normally heard at a ballpark — it was more like a taunt.

23:51 She scored the players, and fans fed her ideas
In her first years with the White Sox, Nancy Faust still played a set repertoire: the national anthem, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, and the hour when fans came in. In her third year she started improvising, playing whatever she saw. When Dick Allen came up, fans would leave the restrooms and popcorn stands, so she played the then-popular Jesus Christ Superstar, and when he hit a home run the place went crazy. Fans sitting around her booth started offering her ideas: one player had worked at a watch counter, the store closed and he got stuck there, so when he came up she played Does Anybody Really Know What Time It Is. She says she was "the soundtrack to whatever was happening," not just scoring the players.

25:52 An opposing pitcher admitted the singing shook his confidence
After that 1977 singalong, one opposing pitcher told reporters: you're standing on the mound, there are men on base, Zisk is in the batter's box, thirty thousand people are singing Kiss It Goodbye, and that shakes your confidence. Nancy Faust later read in a book that players recalling those years said they hated hearing that sound, and winced when they heard na-na-goodbye. And White Sox slugger Richie Zisk said of those same fans: I don't know if they came to see us or we came to see them, but I can tell you it fired us up. Nancy's conclusion: I guess I did have an impact, I just didn't know it at the time.

28:56 She can't read music — it's all by ear
Every song Nancy Faust improvised over her career, she did by ear — she can't read music. Hum a few bars of anything and within seconds she'd play it back on the organ. She retired from the White Sox organist job in 2010, White Sox fan and former president Barack Obama personally wrote to congratulate her on her career, and the booth she occupied for decades is now named after her. She still occasionally comes back for special occasions, like Pope Night, playing Gotta Have Faith and Don't Stop Believing.

item.title: Iron Age Ireland had no Celtic invasion, only trade and language
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
